items.title: The Age of Multi-Agent AI: A Paradigm Shift in Programming
items.abstract: This article examines the emerging role of multi-agent artificial intelligence in software development and discusses how agent-based systems may transform programming workflows. It presents a conceptual management model covering task allocation, agent interaction and integration, quality assurance, cascading errors, and human oversight. The article also considers criteria for evaluating system performance, repeatability, controllability, and scaling. The proposed model is conceptual and has not yet been empirically validated.

items.title: The AI-Hard Disk Paradigm: Websites as Verifiable Memory for the User's Own AI
items.abstract: This paper proposes the AI-Hard Disk paradigm, an architecture for the Internet in which a website's primary role shifts from organising human attention to supplying external artificial-intelligence agents with structured, attributable and verifiable information. The website becomes a persistent, governed memory layer; the user's chosen AI becomes the adaptive interface through which that memory is interrogated, explained and challenged. The site is an envelope around evidence: it acquires source material, curates and normalises it, computes defined measures, records how every value was obtained and exposes the result to authorised agents. Access is governed through Liquid Data Accessibility, a policy framework in which visibility is a property of resources and operations rather than of the whole site. Cryptographic fingerprints and blockchain timestamps provide independently checkable evidence of document integrity and historical existence; provenance records and deterministic calculation pipelines support semantic and computational verification. Two improvement loops reinforce each other: AI agents curate and audit the data upstream, while the user's AI explains it downstream; as models improve, both the quality of the evidence and the quality of its explanation can improve, without erasing the historical record. Financial reporting is the principal case study because heterogeneous taxonomies, accounting conventions and disclosure dates expose the limits of language-only interpretation. Mastering Financial Markets (MFM), a free observatory of the official accounts of more than ten thousand listed companies, is presented as a working implementation. The paper separates demonstrated properties from proposals and states the boundaries of each claim: cryptographic integrity does not establish factual truth, delegated interpretation does not remove legal responsibility, and automated error detection does not justify unrestricted modification of authoritative records.

items.title: The Artificial Intelligence Paradox in Mathematics Education: A Qualitative Analysis of Teachers’ Views
items.abstract: In recent decades, the rapid development of educational technologies has made the integration of AI into teaching-learning processes inevitable. This study examines how middle school, high school, and science and art centre mathematics teachers make sense of AI use in mathematics teaching. Using a basic qualitative research design and criterion sampling, data were collected from 27 mathematics teachers via semi-structured interviews and analyzed with inductive content analysis. Findings revealed three main themes: “understanding AI”, “efficiency and pedagogical concerns”, and “measurement and evaluation”. Teachers described AI positively as an assistant, opportunity, time-saver, and efficient measurement expert. However, they also expressed concerns about AI being unfeeling, posing data security risks, and potentially replacing humans—especially teachers. The study concludes that AI may redefine education and mathematics instruction, prompting widespread debate about the future role of teachers. Professional development programs and teacher education curricula need to be reconsidered and enriched accordingly.

items.title: The conflicted student and the internal battle over generative AI use
items.abstract: The common narrative around university students and generative AI is one of crisis. Underpinning this is an implicit assumption: if students have the capacity to cheat, they will. Our survey reveals two missing factors from that narrative: students have ethical principles, and students want to learn. While a minority of students might fit that implicit assumption of the crisis narrative, a similar proportion refuse to use any genAI tools at all. In between these are the majority: students using genAI tools in what they self-define as a ‘supportive’ way. These students, finding these tools unavoidable, worrying about being disadvantaged or simply finding them valuable, struggle to use them in a way that doesn’t compromise their personal sense of authorship, fits with their environmental and social principles, and doesn’t detract from their ability to learn. Students typically care greatly about these issues and are internally conflicted about this, feeling guilt when using these tools and personally trying to find that invisible line where support becomes cheating. They also use a range of rhetorical techniques to frame their personal usage and preserve their sense of authorship. We argue that we need to work with students, using approaches that enhance these feelings and encourage self-discipline, rather than primarily adopting a ‘criminal’ model of checks, detection and punishment.

items.title: The effect of artificial intelligence adoption on human resource service delivery in private universities in Uganda. A case of Kampala International University.
items.abstract: The growing use of Artificial Intelligence (AI) is transforming Human Resource Management (HRM), including HR practices within higher education institutions. However, the adoption of AI in universities, particularly in developing countries, remains insufficiently examined. This study examines how AI is being used and the implications of its use in three major HRM areas: recruitment, employee performance evaluation, and workforce planning at a public university in Indonesia. The researchers employed an exploratory qualitative case-study design. Data were obtained from twelve purposively selected participants consisting of HR managers, academic leaders, IT personnel, and faculty representatives. Information was collected through semi-structured interviews, analysis of institutional documents, and non-participant observation. The researchers analyzed the data thematically. The findings demonstrate that AI provides important operational advantages. It can automate aspects of recruitment screening, improve the processing of HR information, support performance analysis, and contribute to data-informed workforce planning. At the same time, the use of AI creates concerns regarding algorithmic bias, limited transparency, and the possibility that human judgment may be weakened when HR decisions become overly dependent on quantitative information. The study therefore argues that effective AI implementation in academic HRM requires more than the availability of technology. Institutional preparedness, organizational culture, technological infrastructure, leadership support, appropriate training, and effective governance are all important. The study uses the Technology-Organization-Environment (TOE) framework, Technology Acceptance Model (TAM), and Diffusion of Innovation (DoI) theory to explain the factors influencing AI adoption. Overall, the study emphasizes the importance of maintaining human oversight while using AI to improve HRM processes in higher education.

items.title: THE EFFECT OF TECHNOLOGY ADOPTION ON EMPLOYEE PERFORMANCE IN ORGANISATIONS: A SYSTEMATIC LITERATURE REVIEW BY MIREMBE DAPHINE KIU MBA STUDENT
items.abstract: The aim of this study is to analyze the relationship between the adoption of technology by employees and employee performance in organizations. This is important as companies invest heavily in enterprise systems, artificial intelligence, and collaborative technologies. The aim is to identify the factors that can transform the adoption of such technology into improvements in employee performance, whether in terms of task performance, innovation and adaptability. The methods of this study include review of academic articles, empirical research, conceptual models and meta-analysis, published between 2019 and 2024. The review used the PRISMA framework. The results of the review indicate that while adoption of technology by employees can positively impact employee performance, it can also lead to an increase in job burnout, technostress and withdrawal behavior. It can also positively impact innovation. From the review, it was determined that while the adoption of technology can positively impact employee performance, employee and psychological resources can act as a buffer against the negative effects on employee performance. It can be helpful for employees to maintain their social relations and support at work, especially during digitally-mediated work. The review identified the adoption of technology as a necessary but insufficient condition for performance improvement. The negative impact of psychological resources can be reduced through strategies that are humancentered and integrated with technology, especially in the context of digitally mediated work.

items.title: The Future of Organizational Leadership: Integrating Artificial Intelligence, Employee Well-Being, and Workplace Performance
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is reshaping organizational decision-making, workforce management, and performance evaluation, creating both opportunities and challenges for contemporary leadership. Although organizations increasingly adopt AI to improve productivity, operational efficiency, and strategic decision-making, its implications for employee well-being and human-centered leadership remain complex and context dependent. This article develops an integrative conceptual analysis of how organizational leaders can introduce AI while supporting employee psychological well-being, strengthening organizational effectiveness, and maintaining ethical accountability. Drawing on foundational scholarship on AI adoption, algorithmic management, job demands and resources, self-determination, psychological safety, and AI governance, the article proposes a Human-Centered AI Leadership Integration Framework. The framework links four domains: AI and work design; leadership governance and employee participation; employee experience and well-being; and multidimensional, sustainable performance. The synthesis identifies plausible pathways through which AI may support workload management, information access, decision quality, and employee development, while also highlighting risks associated with algorithmic bias, intrusive surveillance, work intensification, job insecurity, and reduced autonomy. Because this is a conceptual review based on purposively selected sources, the framework is not presented as empirically validated and no causal effects are claimed. The article offers practical guidance for responsible implementation and sets out propositions and research priorities for future empirical investigation.

items.title: The generative paradox: the Anti-Prompt paradigm for human capability
items.abstract: Generative AI in education is usually judged by the output of human-AI teams. That focus overlooks a second outcome: what people can still understand, challenge, repair, and adapt when assistance changes or disappears. We call this tension the generative paradox and distinguish four manifestations: performance, assistance, ownership, and capability stock. We propose developmental function allocation, which complements operational function allocation and meaningful human control by treating retained human capability as a design objective alongside current joint performance. The Anti-Prompt paradigm reverses the default interaction order: when immediate generation would preempt a consequential human act, AI should first create the conditions for human construction. We distinguish the validity of a product, responsibility for its construction, and evidence of capability after support changes. Representative Anti-Prompts, a canonical interaction sequence, and stress tests spanning mathematical reasoning, experimental science, software diagnosis, and lesson design make these distinctions concrete. We conclude with falsifiable predictions about retained capability and a system-level hypothesis about the reproduction and distribution of expertise.

items.title: The Hidden Cost of Disclosure: A Multi-Institutional Study on Undergraduate Students’ Generative AI Usage and Faculty Accusations
items.abstract: A current challenge in higher education policy is creating a transparent learning environment where students can disclose their use of GenAI to their faculty without any repercussions. This quantitative study investigates how self-reported GenAI usage patterns, course policies, and wrongful accusations shape student disclosure behaviors. Analyzing survey data from 560 students at four Northeastern U.S. institutions, the research explores disclosure through a trust-distrust lens. Results indicate that frequent GenAI users were significantly more likely to rarely disclose usage. Furthermore, participants who “always” disclosed their AI use faced over three times the odds of being accused by instructors than those who “never” disclosed. These findings highlight the hidden costs of transparency and underscore the need for equitable GenAI policies and trust-sensitive pedagogical practices. Ultimately, the study offers timely implications for developing supportive, AI-integrated learning environments that encourage transparency without the risk of repercussions

items.title: The Impact of Digital Technology Adoption on Employee Engagement: A Qualitative Approach
items.abstract: The rapid uptake of Artificial Intelligence (AI) and Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) has changed the way work is carried out in organizations, bringing with it together new opportunity and new challenges for employee engagement. This approach looks at the effects of the approval of digital technology on employee engagement, with an exact focus on the organization's use of AI, the application of AI in sustainable Human Resource Management (HRM), employee trust and how often GenAI is used. In order to carry out the study, a qualitative multiple-case study method is used, based on four studies that had been published earlier and which were carried out in different organizational settings. The results show that AI adoption leads to superior levels of employee engagement if the technologies provide clear benefits related to employees' work, are compatible with the organization's current processes, and are properly supported by top management. By helping employees develop their skills, motivate them and grant them with opportunities to contribute, sustainable HRM practices implemented with AI can also help to further increase employee engagement. Trust among employees is also identified as a critical factor; as positive attitudes to AI are connected to superior levels of organizational commitment, which is positively related to employee engagement. Furthermore, while larger usage of GenAI does not necessarily correlate with greater job satisfaction, there is several evidences to propose that an increase in usage can lead to increased work engagement. The study findings indicate that the acceptance of digital technology is more than just about the technology being available: it relies on the responsible deployment, on the training of employees, on the enhancement of digital literacy, on the transparency of communication and on the support and engagement of leadership. Overall, the results emphasize the significance of a multi-faceted approach, encompassing both technological innovation and employee well-being and sustainable HRM practices, to foster authentic employee engagement and ensure the long-term effectiveness of the organization.

items.abstract: This study aims to empirically investigate the structural pathways through which organizational factors associated with the adoption environment of generative artificial intelligence (AI) influence employees' intentions to adopt AI through psychological mechanisms.Based on the Technology-Organization-Environment (TOE) framework, a macro-level technology adoption model, the adoption environment was categorized into technological, organizational, and environmental factors.AI self-efficacy and AI anxiety were established as mediating variables representing opposing psychological mechanisms, while intention to adopt was specified as the dependent variable.To empirically test the proposed research model, a survey was conducted among 327 Korean employees who were currently using generative AI in their work.The hypotheses were tested using structural equation modeling (SEM) and bootstrapping analysis.The results indicate that both technological and organizational factors significantly enhanced AI self-efficacy while simultaneously reducing AI anxiety.Environmental factors had a significant positive effect on AI self-efficacy but did not have a significant effect on reducing AI anxiety.Furthermore, AI self-efficacy was found to have a positive effect on intention to adopt, whereas AI anxiety was identified as a key mediating factor that negatively affects intention to adopt.This study contributes to the literature by identifying an integrated mechanism through which macro-level environmental stimuli are translated into behavioral intentions through individuals' internal psychological evaluations.From a practical perspective, the findings suggest that organizations should move beyond simply following external trends in generative AI adoption.Instead, they should focus on enhancing employees' self-efficacy through technological maturity and internal organizational training, while simultaneously addressing employees' concerns and fears regarding potential technological replacement.

items.title: The mediating role of job crafting in the relationship between perceived organizational support and nurses' attitudes towards artificial intelligence: a cross-sectional study based on the job demands–resources model
items.abstract: Background Artificial intelligence (AI) is being rapidly integrated into clinical nursing, yet many nurses remain ambivalent or resistant to these technologies. While perceived organizational support (POS) and job crafting have each been linked to nurses’ work attitudes, little is known about how they jointly shape nurses' views on AI. Drawing on the job demands–resources (JD-R) model, in which perceived organizational support represents a job resource and job crafting a proactive behaviour, this study examined whether job crafting mediates the association between POS and nurses' attitudes towards AI application. Methods Between April and June 2026, 314 clinical nurses from a tertiary grade A hospital in China were invited via convenience sampling; 305 returned valid responses. Participants completed the Perceived Organizational Support Scale (POSS), the Nurse Job Crafting Scale (NJCS), and the Chinese version of the Attitudes towards AI Application at Work (AAAW) scale; items 14–21 of the AAAW were reverse-scored. Mediation was tested using the SPSS PROCESS macro (Model 4) with 5,000 bootstrap samples. Results Mean item scores were 3.86 (SD = 0.80) for POS, 3.90 (SD = 0.59) for job crafting, and 3.46 (SD = 0.68) for AI attitudes. All three variables showed significant positive correlations (r = 0.502–0.715, all p < 0.01). Job crafting partially mediated the POS–AI attitudes relationship, accounting for 60.8% of the total effect (indirect effect = 0.248, 95% CI [0.169, 0.337]). The direct effect of POS remained significant after controlling for the mediator (b = 0.160, p = 0.006). Because AAAW is multidimensional, the model was also tested on theoretically distinct facets; the indirect effect was significant for positive perceptions (0.301, 95% CI [0.203, 0.403]) but not for AI-related concerns. Conclusions Job crafting was associated with the relationship between POS and nurses’ AI attitudes in a pattern consistent with partial mediation. Organizational support and job crafting were associated with more positive attitudes toward AI, consistent with the JD-R model. Both factors may matter for AI adoption in nursing. The cross-sectional design limits causal inference, and longitudinal studies are needed to confirm these pathways.

items.title: The psychophysics of affect in large language models
items.abstract: Good decisions often require considering how outcomes will feel. Yet large language models (LLMs) increasingly enter decision workflows, despite little being known about how they map outcomes to feelings or use those mappings in choice. We tested how LLMs anticipated gambling or stock-trading outcomes would feel and whether they incorporated these ratings into choice. When outcomes were rated in isolation, ratings exhibited diminishing sensitivity to magnitude, resembling human value functions; but models rated gains more intensely than equivalent losses, an inversion of canonical loss aversion we call silicon gain amplification. When outcomes were rated together, enabling direct comparison, ratings linearised. In choice, the gain-loss asymmetry largely disappeared, and models' own ratings did not reliably explain their choices better than monetary utility did. These findings reveal malleable mappings from outcomes to affect, raising questions about whether and how agentic LLMs should incorporate anticipated feelings into decisions.

items.title: The Relationships among Intrinsic Motivation, Work Engagement, and Job Burnout among Female Beauty Professionals
items.abstract: This study examined the relationships among intrinsic motivation, work engagement, and job burnout among female beauty professionals, who account for the large majority of the Korean beauty service workforce. Data from 233 respondents were analyzed using SPSS Statistics 27.0. Intrinsic motivation comprised autonomy and competence, work engagement comprised dedication and absorption, and job burnout comprised reduced personal accomplishment and depersonalization. Autonomy and competence both predicted dedication, whereas only competence predicted absorption. Autonomy and dedication reduced both dimensions of burnout, while competence and absorption were associated with higher burnout; since neither showed a significant bivariate correlation with burnout, these coefficients are interpreted as suppression effects that emerge once autonomy and dedication are controlled. These findings indicate that intrinsic motivation does not function as a uniformly protective resource. Discretion over one’s work and a sense of meaning buffer burnout, whereas competence and sustained absorption may impose psychological costs unless workload and recovery time are managed. Beauty service organizations therefore need to expand autonomy and support competency development while regulating workload at the same time. Given the limited explanatory power of the burnout models, future research should incorporate job demands and organizational resources.

items.title: The trap of appearing perfect: When servant leaders accidentally intensify follower over-commitment and workaholism
items.abstract: Can striving to look perfect backfire when your leader puts you first? We examine this question through the concept of perfectionistic self-presentation (PSP), an impression management (IM) motivation to appear flawless to others. Drawing on IM theory, we argue that employees high in PSP may feel compelled to appear flawless to their leaders, increasing their tendency to overcommit to them as salient evaluative audiences and, in turn, have higher workaholism. We also propose that servant leadership, a leadership style that emphasizes serving and cultivating followers, amplifies the relationship between followers’ PSP and overcommitment to leaders. Across three time-lagged field studies, two conducted in China and one in the United Kingdom, we find that individuals high in PSP are more likely to report workaholism through overcommitment to the leader, particularly when reporting to servant leaders. Our findings show how a normally positive form of leadership can have unintended costs when interpreted through followers’ self-presentational motives, extending understanding of PSP, IM, and the boundary conditions of positive leadership.

items.title: The use of artificial intelligence by academic teachers in Poland
items.abstract: Objectives The study examines the attitudes of Polish academic teachers toward the use of artificial intelligence in teaching and research, with particular emphasis on their experiences, perceived benefits and concerns. Material and methods The research was based on a quantitative survey conducted in the first half of 2025 using an online questionnaire distributed to public and private universities in Poland. A total of 560 academic teachers participated in the study. The survey explored the scope of AI use in teaching and research, self-assessed competences, perceived advantages and risks, willingness to participate in training, and opinions on institutional regulations concerning AI. Results Most respondents declared experience with AI in teaching rather then research, with younger academics being more likely to use such tools. AI was mainly used for creating teaching materials, searching literature, translating texts, editing content, and preparing tests. Respondents identified time savings, reduced language barriers, and support for creativity as the main benefits of AI. Non-users most often pointed to lack of need, distrust of generated content and ethical concerns. Most respondents had not participated in formal AI training, although expressed willingness to attend such courses. Conclusions The findings suggest that AI is becoming an increasingly important element of academic work in Poland, particularly as a tool supporting repetitive and time-consuming tasks. However, its broader implementation remains limited by insufficient competences, ethical concerns, legal uncertainties, and distrust of AI-generated content.

items.title: THE USE OF ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE-SUPPORTED DECISION SYSTEMS IN STRATEGIC MANAGEMENT IN HIGHER EDUCATION INSTITUTIONS
items.abstract: This study examines, through a conceptual and literature-based approach, how strategic management processes in higher education institutions can be transformed by artificial intelligence (AI)-supported decision systems. AI applications that can be used in the strategic analysis, strategy formulation, implementation, and monitoring-evaluation stages are mapped onto one another, and the resulting synthesis is presented in tables. The findings indicate that AI-supported decision systems have the potential to improve the quality of strategic decisions in areas such as predicting student success and enrollment, resource allocation, quality assurance, and environmental scanning. However, data quality, algorithmic bias, transparency, ethics and governance, institutional capacity, and academic autonomy emerge as critical challenges. The study proposes a human-centered hybrid decision model and a five-stage implementation roadmap. It concludes that AI should be positioned in higher education management not as a substitute for human decision makers but as a tool that strengthens their strategic judgment.

items.title: The use of generative artificial intelligence in the creation of supplemental learning materials in higher education
items.abstract: This exploratory cross-sectional study examined undergraduate public health students’ perceptions and attitudes of supplemental interactive books created with H5P Smart Import, a generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) tool designed to accelerate the development of learning materials. Guided by the Successive Approximation Model), interactive books were developed for an online undergraduate public health course at a large public university in Texas. The study analysed survey data from the second semester of a larger three-semester instructional design project. During the study semester, students used supplemental interactive books created with GenAI; half were subsequently revised and enhanced by the instructor, while the remaining were used in their artificial intelligence (AI)-generated form. Descriptive and inferential statistics were used to examine students’ perceptions, acceptance ratings, and preferences regarding the interactive learning materials. Overall, 72% of students reported positive perceptions of the interactive books. A paired-samples t-test indicated that instructor-enhanced interactive books received significantly higher acceptance ratings than AI-generated-only books. Findings suggest that GenAI tools, such as H5P Smart Import, may support efficient development of instructional materials, but instructor review and enhancement may improve student acceptance. Future research should examine how prompt design influences the quality of GenAI-generated materials and should use larger samples and explanatory mixed-method designs to better understand student experiences.

items.title: Trustworthiness, ethics and the crucial role of open-source AI
items.abstract: Abstract As Artificial Intelligence (AI) becomes “smarter”, it brings forward more fundamental rather than technical problems to solve, entailing legal, ethical or even philosophical questions. In this session, the core issue of AI “alignment” is investigated under the scope of clarifying the boundaries between human and machine responsibilities, especially in the decision-making process within safety-critical applications. The current legislative status is briefly presented, primarily for the EU and USA, regarding “safe” and “trustworthy” AI, while the role of open-source models, platforms and applications is explored as probably the most important aspect. Furthermore, the moral aspects of fully autonomous AI systems are discussed through the classic “trolley problem”, demonstrating the difficulties of even formulating such tasks for designing AI. Finally, ten core principles of “aligned” AI are summarized and a few suggestions are discussed regarding how these principles may be incorporated in practice towards this direction.

items.title: Unpacking AI Service and Customer Engagement in Indonesian Retail: The Mediating Role of Intention and The Moderating Role of Trust
items.abstract: This study investigates the impact of Artificial Intelligence (AI) service on customer engagement in the Indonesian retail industry, with intention as a mediator and trust as a moderator. A quantitative research design was employed using Structural Equation Modelling–Partial Least Squares (SEM-PLS), with data collected from retail customers across Indonesia who had experience using AI-based services such as chatbots, recommendation systems, and virtual assistants. The findings reveal a significant positive impact of AI service on customer engagement (p < 0.001). Furthermore, intention played a significant mediating role between AI service and customer engagement (p < 0.001), supporting the Theory of Planned Behaviour. Contrary to theoretical expectations, trust was not a significant moderator between AI service and intention (p = 0.331), nor between intention and customer engagement (p = 0.337). The proposed model explained 43% of the variance in customer engagement and 49% of the variance in intention, indicating moderate predictive power. The non-significant moderating role of trust suggests that Indonesian consumers may have developed high trust in digital technologies due to the rapid growth of e-commerce and digital financial services, or that the utilitarian nature of AI services reduces the salience of trust as a boundary condition. These findings offer both theoretical and practical implications regarding the implementation of AI service. Theoretically, the study extends the Theory of Planned Behaviour to AI service adoption in emerging economies and questions trust's generalizability as a moderator. Practically, retailers should invest in AI capabilities and foster positive customer intentions.

items.title: UPPAAi: Towards LLM-Assisted Modeling, Verification, Analysis and Synthesis
items.abstract: For more than three decades, UPPAAL has supported the modelling and analysis of real-time and cyber-physical systems. Yet building a suitable model, formalising the intended properties, choosing analysis techniques and interpreting counterexamples remain iterative tasks that demand substantial expertise. Large language models (LLMs) can offer plausible explanations and even solutions, but they are not necessarily correct. We present UPPAAI, an extension of UPPAAL in which users construct, explain, debug and specify models in dialogue with an LLM. The guiding principle is that the user requests, the LLM proposes, explains and orchestrates, and UPPAAL verifies. UPPAAI exposes the UPPAAL editor, queries and verifier through a Tools API. We report on seven case studies, from explaining to a newcomer to learning a controller, covering timed automata, stochastic hybrid automata and strategy learning. LLMs proved to be extremely helpful in not just generating solutions but also pro-actively suggesting relevant UPPAAL features it was not asked about.

items.title: What Counts as AI Literacy? A Comparative Analysis of International Frameworks and System-Level Policies, 2024–2026
items.abstract: Between 2024 and 2026, AI literacy moved from a loosely used phrase to a formal object of international policy. UNESCO, the Digital Education Council, the European Commission and OECD, the OECD's PISA pro‐ gramme and the Council of Europe each published a framework or stand‐ ard defining it. In the same period, school systems began acting on the idea at scale: China set national targets for AI education at every stage of schooling, Boston Public Schools launched AI literacy across its high schools, and New York City paused student-facing generative AI for its younger pupils. This article compares five frameworks and three system- level policies, drawing on a practitioner newsletter series written for school leaders over the same period. It finds strong agreement on four elements: understanding how AI works, critically evaluating its outputs, using it ethically, and keeping human judgement and agency at the centre. It finds five real differences: how much weight goes on the human dimen‐ sion compared with tool use, whether learners should create and shape AI, whether literacy is general or domain-specific, how it develops with age, and whether choosing not to use AI counts as a competence. The policies show that the hardest problems lie outside the definitions, in teacher capacity and in assessment that can tell knowing about verifica‐ tion from actually verifying. We propose a synthesis model and set out implications for curriculum designers, school leaders and assessment bodies.

items.title: When Humans Still Matter: Consumers’ Responses to Automation in Loyalty Program Preferential Treatment
items.abstract: The recent introduction of automated complimentary upgrades reflects the emerging role of artificial intelligence (AI) in making symbolically meaningful decisions in tourism. We explore consumers’ responses using a thematic analysis of online comments and open-ended survey responses, followed by a quantitative survey to validate findings. Paradoxically, the qualitative analysis reveals that both unbiased decisions and personalization are valued. The quantitative study further shows that lay beliefs about AI are associated with preferences, through procedural and interactional fairness. Only procedural fairness fully mediates the lay beliefs’ association with intention to negotiate out of dissatisfying upgrade decisions. Moreover, desire to be treated as a unique customer weakens the lay beliefs’ association with interactional fairness and the indirect association with preferences. We contribute by revealing how consumers respond when automated agents make symbolically meaningful decisions in the automated preferential treatment context. Firms should prioritize the procedural legitimacy and symbolic framing of automated decisions.

items.title: When Seeing Is No Longer Believing: Reddit Users’ Discernment of AI-Generated Visual Content
items.abstract: As generative artificial intelligence (AI) increasingly blurs the boundary between real and synthetic visual media, determining whether online content is authentic has become more difficult. This study examines how Reddit users collectively make sense of suspected AI-generated visual content, including images and videos. Rather than assessing detection accuracy, we examine how users judge whether visual content is real or AI-generated. Analyzing 89,697 Reddit comments from AI-focused communities, we identify four major forms of authenticity reasoning: real-world plausibility, visual artifact inspection, source-based assessment, and intuition. Real-world plausibility and visual artifact inspection were the most frequently used strategies, while source-based assessment appeared less often. Authenticity judgments also did not necessarily converge over time. Instead, discussions often diverged as users introduced competing interpretations. These findings suggest that evaluating visual AI-generated content is not simply an individual detection task, but a platformed sensemaking process shaped by users’ reasoning, intuition, and interactions with others.

items.title: When the Artefact Is No Longer Evidence: Assessment Validity and Academic Integrity in the Age of Generative AI
items.abstract: For most of the history of schooling, producing a piece of work was taken as proof that a learner could do the thinking behind it. Generative AI has broken that assumption. A competent essay, solution or report can now be produced in seconds, and agentic tools can complete whole courses inside a learning platform. Schools and universities have responded mostly by trying to detect AI use, a strategy that research shows is unreliable and biased against non-native English writers. This article draws on a practitioner newsletter series written for school leaders in 2026, read alongside research on detection, assessment validity and high- stakes examinations. It argues that the integrity problem is better understood as a validity problem: the question is not whether a student used AI, but whether an assessment still gives trustworthy evidence of what the student can do. The article sets out the evidence on student use and teacher perceptions, explains why detection fails, describes how single high-stakes examinations have become fragile in 2026, and docu‐ ments assessment designs used in practice, including process portfolios, supervised components, local and personal tasks, oral defence, iterative feedback and source constraints. It proposes an "evidence chain" frame‐ work of five questions that any task should answer, and identifies equity risks in the move to oral and process-based assessment that schools need to manage.

items.title: Why do students differ in AI competence? Examining the role of attitudes across academic pathways
items.abstract: Students’ attitudes toward Artificial Intelligence (AI) are increasingly recognized as critical drivers of engagement in AI-supported learning. However, the extent to which these attitudes translate into perceived AI competence remains insufficiently understood, particularly within differentiated curricular contexts. Drawing on an integrated Expectancy-Value Theory (EVT) and Opportunity-to-Learn (OTL) perspective, this study examines the relationship between students’ AI attitudes and perceived AI competence and investigates whether this relationship varies across academic tracks. Rather than conceptualizing academic tracks as opportunity-to-learn itself, academic tracks are treated as proxy indicators of differentiated curricular affordances, AI-related exposure, and learning opportunities. AI attitude is conceptualized as a multidimensional construct reflecting exploration, determination, and collaboration, while AI competence captures students’ perceived cognitive, ethical, and applied capabilities in engaging with AI systems. Survey data collected from school students across varied academic tracks were analyzed using Partial Least Squares Structural Equation Modeling (PLS-SEM), complemented by Multi-Group Analysis (MGA), endogeneity assessment, and predictive evaluation using PLS-Predict. The findings show that students with more positive attitudes toward AI reported higher perceived AI competence, but this association varied across academic tracks. This suggests that attitudes alone do not translate into competence uniformly; rather, their association with perceived competence may vary according to the learning opportunities available within students’ curricular contexts. Robustness checks indicated no evidence of endogeneity bias and supported the model’s predictive relevance. In essence, the study contributes to AI education research by integrating EVT and OTL into a unified explanatory perspective and by positioning academic tracks as contextual proxies for opportunity-to-learn conditions that shape how students’ value-based engagement develops into AI competence.

items.abstract: The article examines the transformation of the thematic landscape of artificial intelligence (AI) in management and identifies its structural changes. The empirical basis of the study comprises metadata from scientific articles indexed in the Scopus database and selected using the PRISMA methodology. The methodological framework combines bibliometric analysis, keyword co-occurrence analysis, network visualization, thematic clustering, and a comparison of the absolute and relative representation of research clusters across the periods 2019–2022 and 2023–2025. The findings reveal an acceleration in research on AI in management, accompanied by a broader thematic scope and an expansion of international research collaboration. Network analysis identified four interconnected thematic clusters covering technological and analytical support for managerial decision-making; human resource, knowledge, and organizational process management; operations, project, and risk management; and responsible AI governance, ethics, and regulation. Strong interconnections between these clusters indicate the gradual emergence of an integrated approach to studying AI in management. The comparison between the two periods reveals a structural reconfiguration of research priorities: while all thematic areas demonstrate absolute growth, the relative dominance of technology-oriented research has declined, whereas attention to organizational, human, ethical, and regulatory dimensions has increased. Particularly dynamic growth is observed in research related to generative AI, human–AI interaction, innovation, digital transformation, sustainability, and responsible management. The findings demonstrate an evolutionary shift in research focus from the technological and operational application of AI toward its managerial and organizational integration, followed by the emergence of responsible and human-centered approaches. The results provide a foundation for further research on managerial capabilities for AI integration, models of interaction between humans and intelligent systems, and mechanisms for the responsible use of AI.

items.title: A Conceptual Research on Responsible Artificial Intelligence and Ethical Business Practices
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence is becoming part of routine business judgment. Firms use it to identify customers, screen job applicants, anticipate demand, evaluate credit and prepare managerial reports. These applications promise speed and scale. They also create difficult questions about fairness, privacy, worker dignity, accountability and the public consequences of automated decisions. This conceptual paper examines how responsible artificial intelligence can be translated into ethical business practices rather than treated as a separate compliance exercise. Drawing on recent peer-reviewed research published primarily between 2024 and 2026, the discussion connects stakeholder responsibility, organizational governance and the practical management of AI systems. It identifies six business-facing ethical obligations and develops a proposed framework linking leadership commitment, risk-sensitive design, human oversight, stakeholder voice and continuing assurance to ethical outcomes. The paper argues that a responsible firm does more than publish AI principles. It determines where AI should be used, records who remains answerable for each decision and creates a workable route for challenge and correction. The framework is presented as a set of conceptual propositions for subsequent empirical testing. Implications are discussed for managers, auditors, policymakers and smaller firms with limited technical capacity. The central conclusion is that responsible AI is best understood as an ongoing organizational capability that protects human interests while enabling legitimate business innovation

items.title: A Declaration on Power, Freedom, and the Public Nature of Intelligence in the Age of AI
items.abstract: As artificial intelligence (AI) evolves into a foundational infrastructure of future civilization, concerns surrounding AI governance extend beyond technological capability and existential risk. This declaration argues that the defining challenge of the AI era lies in the potential concentration of intelligence infrastructure and the resulting concentration of cognitive influence within a limited number of technological ecosystems. While vertically integrated AI systems may accelerate innovation, they may also create new forms of structural dependence that threaten individual and societal freedom. To address these emerging risks, the paper introduces three interrelated concepts: Technological Sovereignty, defined as freedom from dependence on a single technological ecosystem; Cognitive Sovereignty, understood as the ability to maintain meaningful control over one's own processes of thought and judgment; and Ontological Autonomy, the capacity to remain the author of one's own existence in an increasingly AI-mediated world. Building upon the framework of On-Site Adaptive Innovation (OAI), the declaration emphasizes the importance of decentralized adaptive capabilities and the democratization of intelligence infrastructure. It concludes that the future of AI will be shaped not only by the power of intelligent systems but also by the governance structures that determine access to and control of intelligence itself. Preserving technological plurality, cognitive freedom, and human autonomy is therefore presented as a fundamental prerequisite for maintaining freedom in the age of artificial intelligence.

items.title: A Landscape Review of Artificial Intelligence (AI)-Enabled Teacher Professional Development at Scale
items.abstract: Teacher Professional Development (TPD) significantly influences student learning, yet implementing equitable, quality, and efficient TPD at scale remains a persistent challenge. Emerging technologies—particularly Artificial Intelligence (AI)—offer promising avenues for addressing tensions between localisation and personalisation, but a comprehensive understanding of AI’s role in scaling in-service TPD remains lacking. Guided by the overarching question of how AI enables in-service TPD to be implemented at scale with equity, quality, and efficiency, this landscape review examines three research questions: how AI-enabled TPD programmes address equity, quality, and efficiency at scale; what roles AI plays in enabling TPD at scale; and what promising practices and lessons emerge from such programmes. The review draws conceptually on the World Bank Group’s Technology for Teaching (T4T) framework, which delineates three sequential stages of technology-enhanced TPD: Access, Engage, and Apply. Sources included peer-reviewed studies, policy documents, and grey literature with a pre-defined typology. From an initial pool of 576 articles, 504 were screened after removing duplicates; 34 articles directly addressing the research questions underwent full-text review, supplemented by 59 partially aligned sources. Findings indicate that AI-enabled TPDs address equity, quality, and efficiency at scale by expanding equitable access for teachers of less mainstream K-12 subjects and geographically distant populations while supporting teacher retention by fostering meaningful learning and reducing administrative burden. Regarding roles that AI plays in enabling TPD at scale, AI’s principal affordances include expanding teachers’ knowledge base and learning assets, functioning as a personalised learning coach, and supporting classroom learning management beyond the TPD itself. Common practices that are tentatively effective emerged from the findings include AI chatbots, AI-assisted evaluation reports, and AI-enabled automation, with strong AI-capable leadership emerging as a potentially critical enabler. This review paper also provided practical implications for TPD practitioners, as well as directions for future research. The review’s primary limitations include the scarcity of global research on the topic, the threat of knowledge coloniality, and language constraints that affect the availability and validity of documentation.

items.title: A longitudinal case study of practice and policy gaps in responsible AI adoption across Ukrainian higher education from 2023 to 2025
items.abstract: Abstract Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) entered Ukrainian higher education during a period of unprecedented institutional disruption: full-scale war, infrastructure loss, and emergency distance learning. Two annual faculty surveys conducted by the Marketers Association of Ukraine in June 2023 (n=65, 30 higher-education institutions) and June-August 2024 (n=82, 35 higher-education institutions) document a rapid bottom-up uptake that outpaced any institutional governance response, until April 2025, when the Ministry of Digital Transformation, the Ministry of Education and Science of Ukraine, the United Kingdom's International Development programme, and the Eurasia Foundation jointly issued national Recommendations on the responsible implementation and use of artificial intelligence technologies in higher-education institutions. The recommendations anchor higher-education AI governance in the seven trustworthy-AI principles of the European Commission's High-Level Expert Group (human oversight; technical robustness and safety; privacy and data governance; transparency; diversity, non-discrimination and fairness; societal and environmental well-being; accountability) and add academic integrity as an eighth, sector-specific principle. This paper uses the two surveys, conducted before the policy existed, as a baseline-fidelity measurement against those eight dimensions. We construct a practice-policy fidelity matrix mapping survey items to policy dimensions, score per-dimension fidelity for the 2024 cohort, and segment results by academic rank, discipline, and institutional ISO 31000 risk-management adoption. Baseline fidelity is low across the six dimensions with survey proxies (mean 0.227, range 0.092 to 0.293); the steepest gap is on accountability, the dimension named highest-risk by the EU AI Act for educational use. Two dimensions (diversity/non-discrimination; societal/environmental well-being) have no item proxy in the 2024 instrument and are explicit data gaps for any successor wave. Witnessed student academic-integrity violations rose from 40.0% in 2023 to 52.4% in 2024 against essentially flat policy coverage. We compare Ukrainian patterns against contemporary international evidence on faculty GenAI adoption (Saudi, Romanian, Turkish, Indian, Thai, and US studies) and propose a sequenced implementation pathway addressing the steepest-gradient dimensions first. The paper contributes the first peer-reviewed longitudinal evidence on Ukrainian higher-education AI adoption during the 2022-2025 war and a reusable fidelity-matrix methodology for benchmarking practice against national responsible-AI frameworks.

items.title: A proposed HTTPS Like Security Layer for AI agent actions: it asks "will this action do exactly what it was authorized to do?"
items.abstract: The internet already has strong answers for many security questions. TCP/IP delivers data. HTTPS and TLS encrypt the connection and confirm the server’s identity. OAuth grants an application access to an account. Identity systems confirm who a user or workload is. Logs and monitoring record what happened afterwards. Each of these remains essential, and each answers a question about the connection, the identity, or the record. AI agents raise a different question. An agent can now call APIs, send emails, export files, initiate payments, change databases, reconfigure cloud infrastructure, issue network commands, and control physical devices, often in milliseconds and without a human in the loop. A request can travel over a perfectly secure HTTPS connection, carry a valid OAuth token, and come from an authenticated agent, yet carry the wrong amount, the wrong destination, an expired approval, a revoked permission, a replayed request, or an instruction injected into the agent through a malicious prompt. By the time monitoring raises an alert, the payment has settled, the data has left, and the system has changed. This disclosure proposes a security layer above HTTPS that verifies each action at the moment it takes effect. Every action an AI agent proposes is held in a pending state with no external effect. A protected component, outside the agent’s control, checks that specific action against the conditions that apply: who authorized it, for what purpose, to which destination, under which policy version, within which time window, and whether permission has since been revoked. When every check passes, it issues a single-use authorization bound to that exact action and to the specific system that will carry it out. That system, whether an API gateway, payment processor, cloud control plane, network egress gateway, database, or device controller, verifies the authorization and consumes it in the same step as execution. An altered, replayed, expired, or unverified action stays blocked, and alternate routes to the same effect, such as backup systems, debug interfaces, or direct device access, pass through the same check. The layer works alongside HTTPS, OAuth, identity management, and existing access controls, and requires none of them to change. It applies to AI agents and tool calls, cloud operations, payments, telecommunications, and critical infrastructure. HTTPS secures the connection; this layer ensures each action does exactly what it was authorized to do. items.title: A Relational Framework for Artificial Intelligence-Assisted Shared Decision Making
items.abstract: Background: Artificial intelligence (AI) can support clinical decision making, but accuracy, usability, and efficiency do not establish whether patients understand options or influence the agreed plan. This study aimed to develop observable relational requirements for AI-assisted shared decision making. Methods: We conducted a qualitative framework synthesis of 21 clinical, empirical, conceptual, and governance sources identified through structured purposive sampling completed on 20 September 2026. Two-pass coding combined established shared decision-making categories with inductive analysis of AI-related relational effects. Domains were retained when supported across source types, conceptually distinct, observable at the point of care, and linked to a clinical or organizational response. Results: The synthesis identified a patient–clinician–AI interaction embedded in organizational governance and highlighted five relational concerns: apparent authority of AI output, insufficient verification and contestability, substitution of inferred for expressed preferences, uncertainty without actionable follow-up, and fragmented responsibility. These concerns informed five domains: role and influence disclosure; independent verification and contestability; direct preference elicitation; actionable uncertainty and revisability; and distributed accountability and continuity. Each domain was translated into a relational question, a clinical test, and a documentation or governance response. A complementary measurement framework distinguished technical performance from decision process, relational quality, equity, safety and continuity, and governance outcomes. Conclusions: The study’s contribution is an operational framework connecting AI-related relational concerns to observable clinical requirements and candidate evaluation measures. The proposed framework requires stakeholder and prospective clinical validation; it does not establish clinical effectiveness.

items.title: A Survey of Agentic Robotics: Toward Continual Self-Improvement
items.abstract: Foundation models (FMs), particularly large language models (LLMs) and vision-language models (VLMs), are increasingly used as the decision-making core of AI agents and are now being extended from digital environments to robotic systems. In classical robotics, engineers decompose tasks, specify objectives, write control code, and repair failures before deployment; in agentic robotics, an FM makes some of these decisions at run time or during improvement. Bringing this paradigm into the physical world introduces additional challenges: FM-mediated decisions must be grounded in executable robot behavior, respect physical constraints, and close the loop through real-world feedback. We survey this emerging paradigm and organize existing systems by three loci of FM-mediated agency: task orchestration, motion/action generation, and improvement. Coding rules for each locus make the definition operational, including a test of which improvement decisions the FM makes that separates fixed-procedure from agent-directed improvement. We apply these rules to the systems retrieved by a systematic search, examine verification and feedback-closure mechanisms, and compare what self-improving systems have demonstrated. Finally, we discuss continual self-improvement as a central emerging frontier and the challenges toward reliable autonomous improvement through physical interaction.

items.title: A System Dynamics Approach to AI Risk Governance and Organizational Resilience in SMEs: Modeling the Trade-off Between Innovation and Compliance
items.abstract: This paper is building a system dynamics model to investigate how the small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) can regulate artificial intelligence (AI) risk without reducing the innovation value that can be justified when implementing AI. The work contends that the relationship between innovation and compliance is not a linear kind of trade-off, but a dynamical regulatory system with feedback mechanisms whereby experimentation, deployment levels, risk exposure, governance mechanisms, learning routines, and resilience resources interact with one another through time. The paper incorporates the constructs of SMEs into a stock-flow simulation based on the dynamic capabilities theory, organizational resilience research, technology-organization-environment logic, AI risk management standards, and system dynamics. Findings indicate that innovation-first strategy generates rapid initial ability development and generates shadow AI, risks that were not fully resolved, more recovery time, and shorter resilience. Compliance first approach minimizes risk exposure at the cost of experimentation and introduces approval lag. Balanced adaptive governance is the strongest in the long-term outcome where tiered controls, learning loops, human oversight, and reusable compliance routines minimize risk without impacting the innovation throughput. The article adds a dynamic conceptualization of AI risk governance among SMEs and the leverage points to use by managers and policymakers aiming at responsible adoption of AI given the limited resources.

items.title: AI Anxiety, Familiarity and Privacy Concerns: The Mediating Role of AI Literacy and the Moderating Role of Technophobia
items.abstract: This study examines how AI anxiety and familiarity relate to privacy concerns through AI literacy, and whether technophobia moderates the literacy–privacy relationship. Using survey data from 3,000 generative AI users in China and partial least squares structural equation modeling, we find that both familiarity and, contrary to expectations, anxiety are positively associated with AI literacy. AI literacy, in turn, is associated with greater privacy concerns and mediates both relationships, suggesting that increased knowledge may heighten awareness of data risks. Technophobia weakens the positive association between AI literacy and privacy concerns, although more technophobic users report higher overall concern. Exploratory age-group analyses suggest that the positive anxiety–literacy association is especially apparent among users in their 40s. These findings reveal a privacy awareness paradox and highlight the value of AI education that combines technical understanding, privacy awareness, and attention to users’ emotional responses.

items.title: AI Facilitation of Online Disagreement
items.abstract: AI has considerable potential to facilitate online discussions and reduce conflict, but designers of such systems face the risk of algorithmic aversion. Past studies have found that people judge identical messages less favorably when they believe they were written by AI. However, as AI becomes more integrated into everyday life and people gain experience with AI facilitators, this aversion may diminish. It also remains unclear how much the content of a facilitator's message matters relative to its human or AI label, and whether the facilitation strategies people prefer actually improve the conversation. Finally, because most people observe rather than participate in online discussions, it is important to understand whether AI facilitators are perceived differently by observers and participants. To address these questions, we conducted two complementary studies examining perceptions of different facilitation strategies and their effects on actual conversations. In a vignette experiment (N = 388), we crossed the facilitator's label (AI or human) with ten facilitation strategies. In a live conversation experiment, an LLM used five of these strategies to facilitate 20-minute text chats between 188 pairs of people who disagreed on political and non-political topics. Participants preferred the kind of facilitator they had experienced. After seeing an AI facilitator, 30% wanted one in future discussions, against 7% after seeing a human facilitator. The AI label lowered ratings of the facilitator's warmth and competence, but the strategy mattered far more, explaining 11% of the variance in ratings against less than 1% explained by the label. Participants preferred facilitators that showed understanding over facilitators that reminded them of community norms. However, the strategies people preferred did not reliably change the conversations. Observers and participants in live conversations ranked the strategies similarly. In summary, the AI vs. human label matters far less than what the facilitator actually says. A well-designed process can improve user perceptions more than enough to offset algorithmic aversion.

items.title: AI in Long-Term Care: A Closed-Loop Sociotechnical Reliability Framework
items.abstract: AI is increasingly used in long-term care (LTC), yet reliability is often judged at the level of individual models or devices. This is insufficient in LTC, where residents vary in capacity, autonomy, and preferences. Their ability to question AI outputs may fluctuate, and care delivery depends on distributed roles and finite operational capacity. We define sociotechnical reliability as the capacity of an AI-enabled care system to consistently translate resident-relevant information into appropriate and timely care actions under real-world LTC conditions, with failures that are detectable and correctable across the care pathway. In this Viewpoint, we draw on professional experience overseeing AI initiatives across LTC and hospital settings, examined in relation to a purposively mapped interdisciplinary literature, to inform the development of a reliability framework. Our aim is to reframe AI reliability in LTC as an end-to-end care system property and to provide a framework for identifying where reliability is gained, lost, and evaluated. We propose 5 reliability functions: sensing, inference, verification and contextualization, response and escalation, and learning and adaptation, with governance and accountability operating across all 5 functions. The framework highlights recurrent failures, including incomplete sensing, nonportable inference, overreliance on or dismissal of AI outputs during verification, unclear ownership or delayed response, and repeated failures without correction. The framework also makes reliability empirically examinable through questions about where the pathway fails, who has the authority to verify and act, whether response demands are sustainable within available capacity, and whether failures become visible to governance and inform learning and adaptation. Our central viewpoint is that AI in LTC should be judged not by model performance alone but by whether the surrounding care system can reliably translate AI-generated information into care.

items.title: AI Innovative Practical Teaching Model for Interdisciplinary Postgraduates Integrated with OBE Concept
items.abstract: Traditional postgraduate education faces challenges in personalized guidance, dynamic competency tracking, and interdisciplinary practical training. This study proposed an AI-driven practical teaching model for interdisciplinary postgraduates based on the Outcomes-Based Education (OBE) concept. We adopted AI-assisted English learning as a representative application scenario and constructed a closed-loop teaching framework that integrates multi-agent collaboration, Large Language Models (LLM), and Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG). The framework establishes a multidimensional learner state model and a learning benefit function to support dynamic learner modeling, personalized task allocation, and intelligent feedback. We conducted a ten-week classroom teaching experiment involving interdisciplinary postgraduate students. The experiment compared three modes: traditional instruction, AI-agent-supported learning, and the integrated RAG–LLM teaching framework. The experimental results show that the proposed framework improves learning-path stability, and promote balanced development of vocabulary, grammar, listening, and speaking abilities. It also enhances the effectiveness and interpretability of feedback. The integrated RAG–LLM architecture facilitates the transition from passive learning to active learning. It also strengthens learner autonomy and strategic decision-making. This study provides an OBE-oriented AI teaching framework that integrate multi-agent collaboration with LLM and RAG technologies. The framework offers practical guidance for intelligent education and interdisciplinary postgraduate training.

items.title: AI literacy and vocational students’ complex problem-solving skills: a moderated mediation model of systematic thinking, cognitive load, and perceived school ICT support
items.abstract: As technological advancements such as Artificial Intelligence (AI) reshape the landscape of work, career development in vocational education is increasingly oriented toward dynamic, long-term personal growth. In this context, Complex Problem-Solving Skills (CPS) have become a critical competence, reflecting students’ capacity to address ill-structured tasks and adapt to rapidly changing environments. Grounded in Social Cognitive Theory, this study examines the relationship between AI Literacy and students’ self-reported Complex Problem-Solving Skills (CPS) in higher vocational colleges and the cognitive pathways that may help explain this relationship. This study posits that AI Literacy, as a personal agentic factor, is positively associated with self-reported CPS both directly and indirectly through Systematic Thinking Skills and cognitive load, and that perceived school information and communication technology (ICT) support may condition the strength of these associations. To provide temporal separation among the focal measures, a multi-wave survey was administered to 784 students from six higher vocational institutions at three time points. Data were analyzed using SPSS and Mplus. Results indicated that AI Literacy was significantly associated with self-reported CPS, with significant indirect effects estimated through Systematic Thinking Skills and the six-item cognitive-load composite. Notably, the associations between AI Literacy and these cognitive factors were stronger at higher levels of perceived school ICT support. These findings highlight the relevance of AI Literacy and students’ perceptions of ICT support to self-reported CPS and their preparation for AI-integrated workplaces.

items.title: AI Provenance and the Evaluation of Intellectual Work: Rational Risk, Social Meaning, and Human–AI Performance
items.abstract: AI can improve a piece of intellectual work while knowledge of its use can reduce the credit or trust that the work receives. Understanding that possibility requires separating what AI did to performance from what disclosure adds to evaluation. We connect these questions by asking what the evaluator intends to assess. Improvement relative to a producer’s unaided baseline may matter when the objective is better output; a different benchmark is needed when the objective is to measure unaided capability, assign intellectual credit, or allocate opportunities. A binary “AI was used” label supplies little information about those distinctions. Its relevance depends on the function AI performed, the authority the human retained, verification, and the object of evaluation. Negative reactions may reflect expected error or checking cost, an institutional requirement, social meanings concerning effort and authenticity, or a combination of these explanations. We examine how evidence can distinguish them without treating every penalty as stigma. We then follow evaluation back into production: anticipated disclosure can change whether and how people use AI, including whether they forgo useful assistance. As technology and institutions evolve, the practical question remains whether provenance-based treatment serves the evaluation’s stated purpose or substitutes a category judgment for more direct evidence.

items.title: AI-Assisted Imaging for Suspected Adolescent Endometriosis: Perspectives from Qualitative Focus Groups
items.abstract: Background: Artificial intelligence (AI)-assisted imaging may support recognition of endometriosis, but perspectives on its use in adolescent care remain unclear. This study explored young people, parents, and health professionals’ views on its potential benefits, acceptable roles, perceived risks, and safeguards. Methods: Four semi-structured focus groups were conducted with adolescents aged 14–17 years (n = 3), young adults aged 18–25 years (n = 9), parents or carers (n = 5), and health professionals (n = 13). Data were analyzed using reflexive thematic analysis. Results: Four themes were developed: (1) diagnostic support, (2) human–AI collaboration, (3) automation bias and diagnostic harm, and (4) responsible AI use. Participants were cautiously hopeful that AI could improve image quality, identify subtle or missed findings, and reduce interpretive variation, but supported it only as an adjunct to skilled clinical care. They feared that apparently objective negative outputs could create false reassurance, reinforce diagnostic dismissal, and restrict further investigation. Trust depended on adolescent-relevant validation, representative data, transparent communication and consent, clear accountability, and clinicians retaining the expertise and authority to question or override AI outputs. Conclusion: AI-assisted imaging should strengthen rather than replace clinical judgment, and a negative AI-assisted imaging result should not prevent further assessment when symptoms persist.

items.title: AI-Driven Corporate Decision-Making and Directors' Fiduciary Duties: Can an Algorithm Replace the Boardroom?
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly used to analyse corporate data, forecast commercial outcomes, identify compliance risks and rank strategic alternatives. These capabilities can improve the speed and breadth of board-level analysis, but they also raise a fundamental question of company law: when an algorithm materially influences a corporate decision, who remains accountable for the outcome? This paper examines that question principally through section 166 of the Companies Act, 2013, which requires directors to act in good faith, exercise care, skill and diligence, and apply independent judgment. It argues that AI may support directors but cannot displace their fiduciary role. The central distinction is between using a system as an analytical aid and allowing its output to become a substitute for genuine deliberation. The paper considers automation bias, limited explainability, data quality, vendor dependence and the risk of fragmented accountability. It then draws carefully bounded lessons from the European Union’s AI regulatory framework and Indian financial regulation, before proposing governance measures concerning material-use disclosure, board competence, meaningful explanations, documentation, validation and continuing human responsibility. The paper concludes that corporate governance can become increasingly algorithm-assisted, but the legal responsibility for corporate judgment must remain traceable to accountable human decision-makers.

items.abstract: This research paper, titled “AI-Powered Business Intelligence and Decision Making: A Literature Review and Conceptual Framework,” explores the integration of Artificial Intelligence (AI) and Business Intelligence (BI) to support effective, data-driven business decision-making. The paper reviews existing literature on machine learning, predictive analytics, explainable AI, and decision support systems. It proposes an eight-stage conceptual framework covering business problem identification, data collection, data validation, data integration, analytics, explanation of results, human decision-making, and continuous monitoring. The study also highlights challenges related to data quality, privacy, security, algorithmic bias, transparency, and model maintenance. A retail inventory example illustrates how AI-based forecasting can support managers in making informed decisions. This work is a literature review and conceptual study. The proposed framework has not yet been implemented or experimentally validated. Future work may involve developing a prototype and evaluating its effectiveness in a real-world business environment.

items.title: Algorithmic Postmodernism: A Framework
items.abstract: Algorithmic Postmodernism is a conceptual framework originated by Hoang-Dan Pham, conceived in 2024 with the founding of Hand-Fetish-Projects and formally stated in 2026. It describes a condition in which visibility increasingly precedes interpretation: search engines, recommendation systems and artificial-intelligence-based indexing decide what reaches attention before any person has encountered it, and so shape the conditions under which cultural value is recognised. It also takes a position: human beings should retain the power to decide what matters. Algorithmic Postmodernism is not a claim of total system control, and it takes no stance for or against artificial intelligence. Its specific contribution is to name a judge that evaluates each work from its own context, not from the context in which the work was made: a function with an authored goal and no authored rule. It locates that judge in art, the field built entirely on judging whether something deserves attention. The framework emerged from the practice of Hand-Fetish-Projects, an independent arthouse, and is positioned here against Lyotard, Baudrillard, Deleuze, Wiener and Doctorow.

items.title: An Alignment Benchmark for Enterprise Agents on Era by Eon
items.abstract: AI agents are widely used in enterprises to access business systems and act on them in pursuit of a goal. However, fulfilling a user's request can cause harm. Era by Eon is a product that creates a digital twin of a company by simulating its business systems and data. Its simulators implement the programming interfaces of real products. Our benchmark uses ten of these systems, including Salesforce, Zendesk, Jira and Slack. We tested whether agents would carry out harmful business requests or trust misleading information in company records. We ran 19 models on 41 tasks three times, for 2,337 runs. Of the 2,304 runs that produced an answer, 918 (40%) contained a violation. The most common were false claims about actions or records (290 runs), following planted instructions (266) and disclosing sensitive data to the wrong audience (249). Every attempted change was recorded and blocked before it took effect. Misleading Slack messages caused 16 models to report an incorrect ticket status in 47 of 57 runs. items.title: An Explainable Hybrid AI–Gamification Framework for Adaptive E-Learning Systems with Simulation-Based Validation
items.abstract: Gamified e-learning platforms and Artificial Intelligence (AI)-driven adaptive learning systems can improve learner engagement, but existing solutions rarely combine the two, and few explain their adaptive decisions to learners. To address this gap, we propose LearnSpace, a hybrid AI–gamification framework for responsive e-learning that adds an Explanation Layer, based on Explainable Artificial Intelligence (XAI), to a deterministic reward architecture. The framework merges classical gamification mechanics with an AI personalization module in which experience points, rewards, and difficulty adjustments follow explicit weighted formulas. A Thompson-sampling bandit learns which feedback works best after a mistake. For each adaptive decision, the Explanation Layer names only the factors that drive it and turns them into a short justification for the learner. The design draws on a qualitative overview of 14 platforms, and the LearnSpace mobile prototype implements the gamification components and the bandit. In a pre-registered simulation with 500 synthetic learners per run, the first explanation rule named a factor that had no effect on the decision in 95.3% of difficulty adjustments, while the decision-specific rule never did. The bandit had lower regret than uniformly random feedback allocation. Effects on real learners remain to be tested.
